questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Pulmonary embolism, pulmonary hypertension & sleep apnoea
questions.stem: Which anticoagulant is preferred for pulmonary embolism in a patient with active gastrointestinal malignancy?
options: Warfarin with a target INR of 2 to 3
Low molecular weight heparin or a direct oral anticoagulant with careful bleeding assessment
questions.concept: Cancer-associated thrombosis recurs more often on warfarin, so low molecular weight heparin was long standard; direct oral anticoagulants are now equivalent overall but carry more mucosal bleeding in luminal gastrointestinal and urothelial tumours.
questions.reference: Harrison 21e, Ch. 273 (Deep Venous Thrombosis and Pulmonary Thromboembolism)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Pulmonary embolism, pulmonary hypertension & sleep apnoea
questions.stem: The recommended duration of anticoagulation after a first pulmonary embolism provoked by major surgery is:
questions.concept: A transient major provoking factor that has resolved gives a low recurrence risk, so three months suffices; unprovoked or persistently provoked events warrant extended therapy with periodic reassessment.
questions.reference: Harrison 21e, Ch. 273 (Deep Venous Thrombosis and Pulmonary Thromboembolism)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Pulmonary embolism, pulmonary hypertension & sleep apnoea
questions.stem: Which finding on arterial blood gas is most typical of acute pulmonary embolism?
options: Hypoxaemia with hypocapnia and a raised alveolar-arterial gradient
Normal gases with a metabolic alkalosis
questions.concept: Dead space ventilation and hyperventilation lower carbon dioxide while ventilation-perfusion mismatch widens the gradient; a normal gas result does not exclude embolism, which is why imaging is decided by clinical probability.
questions.reference: Harrison 21e, Ch. 273 (Deep Venous Thrombosis and Pulmonary Thromboembolism)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Pulmonary embolism, pulmonary hypertension & sleep apnoea
questions.stem: In suspected pulmonary embolism with renal impairment precluding contrast, the most appropriate imaging is:
questions.concept: A perfusion or ventilation-perfusion scan avoids iodinated contrast and performs well when the chest radiograph is normal, which is usual in pulmonary embolism without coexisting lung disease.
questions.reference: Harrison 21e, Ch. 273 (Deep Venous Thrombosis and Pulmonary Thromboembolism)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Pulmonary embolism, pulmonary hypertension & sleep apnoea
questions.stem: Which echocardiographic finding identifies intermediate-risk (submassive) pulmonary embolism in a normotensive patient?
options: Right ventricular dilatation and hypokinesis with septal flattening
questions.concept: Right ventricular strain plus a raised troponin defines intermediate-high risk, which warrants monitored anticoagulation with rescue thrombolysis if deterioration occurs rather than routine primary thrombolysis.
questions.reference: Harrison 21e, Ch. 273 (Deep Venous Thrombosis and Pulmonary Thromboembolism)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Pulmonary embolism, pulmonary hypertension & sleep apnoea
questions.stem: Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension should be suspected when:
options: Breathlessness and pulmonary hypertension persist beyond 3 months of adequate anticoagulation after pulmonary embolism
D-dimer remains detectable at one week
There is a family history of asthma
questions.concept: Persisting organised thrombus with vascular remodelling affects a few per cent of survivors, is diagnosed by ventilation-perfusion scanning and pulmonary angiography, and is potentially curable by pulmonary endarterectomy.
questions.reference: Harrison 21e, Ch. 273 (Deep Venous Thrombosis and Pulmonary Thromboembolism)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Pulmonary embolism, pulmonary hypertension & sleep apnoea
questions.stem: Which class of drug is used in group 1 pulmonary arterial hypertension but is harmful in pulmonary hypertension due to left heart disease?
options: Pulmonary vasodilators such as endothelin receptor antagonists and phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors
questions.concept: Selective pulmonary vasodilatation increases flow into a congested left atrium, precipitating pulmonary oedema, so these agents are confined to group 1 disease after right heart catheterisation confirms the classification.
questions.reference: Harrison 21e, Ch. 273 (Deep Venous Thrombosis and Pulmonary Thromboembolism)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Pulmonary embolism, pulmonary hypertension & sleep apnoea
questions.stem: A patient with obstructive sleep apnoea develops daytime hypercapnia and a raised bicarbonate with a body mass index of 45. This indicates:
questions.concept: Awake hypercapnia with obesity and sleep-disordered breathing defines obesity hypoventilation, which carries much higher mortality than obstructive apnoea alone and often needs bilevel rather than continuous positive airway pressure.
questions.reference: Harrison 21e, Ch. 273 (Deep Venous Thrombosis and Pulmonary Thromboembolism)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Pulmonary embolism, pulmonary hypertension & sleep apnoea
questions.stem: Which pattern on polysomnography distinguishes central from obstructive sleep apnoea?
options: Cessation of airflow with continuing thoracoabdominal effort
Cessation of airflow with absent thoracoabdominal effort
questions.concept: Central events reflect loss of respiratory drive so no effort is made, whereas obstructive events show paradoxical effort against a closed upper airway; central apnoea suggests heart failure, opioids or high altitude.
questions.reference: Harrison 21e, Ch. 273 (Deep Venous Thrombosis and Pulmonary Thromboembolism)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Rheumatoid arthritis, SLE & connective tissue disease
questions.stem: Which extra-articular manifestation of rheumatoid arthritis is the commonest cause of death attributable to the disease itself?
questions.concept: Chronic systemic inflammation roughly doubles cardiovascular risk independent of traditional factors, so risk-factor modification and tight disease control are part of standard rheumatoid care.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Rheumatoid arthritis, SLE & connective tissue disease
questions.stem: Before starting methotrexate, which baseline investigations are essential?
options: Full blood count, liver function and creatinine, with a chest radiograph
questions.concept: Methotrexate causes myelosuppression, transaminitis and rarely pneumonitis, and folic acid supplementation with quarterly monitoring reduces toxicity; the baseline film helps interpret later respiratory symptoms.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Rheumatoid arthritis, SLE & connective tissue disease
questions.stem: Which joints are characteristically spared in rheumatoid arthritis?
options: The distal interphalangeal joints and the thoracolumbar spine
questions.concept: Sparing of the distal interphalangeal joints separates rheumatoid arthritis from psoriatic arthritis and osteoarthritis, and only the cervical spine is involved, where atlantoaxial subluxation is a preoperative anaesthetic concern.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Rheumatoid arthritis, SLE & connective tissue disease
questions.stem: A patient with rheumatoid arthritis is to start a tumour necrosis factor inhibitor. Which screening is mandatory first?
options: Screening for latent tuberculosis and hepatitis B
questions.concept: Tumour necrosis factor is essential for granuloma integrity, so blockade reactivates latent tuberculosis; interferon-gamma release assay or tuberculin testing with a chest radiograph, plus hepatitis serology, precedes therapy.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Rheumatoid arthritis, SLE & connective tissue disease
questions.stem: Which pattern of renal involvement in systemic lupus erythematosus most requires urgent immunosuppression?
options: Class IV diffuse proliferative with active urinary sediment
questions.concept: Diffuse proliferative disease has the worst renal prognosis and responds to induction with mycophenolate or cyclophosphamide plus corticosteroids, whereas class VI represents burnt-out scarring where immunosuppression cannot help.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Rheumatoid arthritis, SLE & connective tissue disease
questions.stem: Which antibody in systemic lupus erythematosus is associated with neonatal lupus and congenital heart block?
questions.concept: Anti-Ro crosses the placenta and damages the fetal conduction system between 18 and 24 weeks, so affected pregnancies need serial fetal echocardiography and hydroxychloroquine reduces recurrence.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Rheumatoid arthritis, SLE & connective tissue disease
questions.stem: A patient with systemic sclerosis develops abrupt severe hypertension with acute kidney injury and a microangiopathic blood picture. The treatment of choice is:
options: An ACE inhibitor such as captopril, titrated rapidly
questions.concept: Scleroderma renal crisis is driven by renin release from ischaemic juxtaglomerular apparatus, and ACE inhibition transformed a once-fatal complication; corticosteroids actually increase the risk of precipitating it.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Rheumatoid arthritis, SLE & connective tissue disease
questions.stem: Which autoantibody in systemic sclerosis predicts the greatest risk of interstitial lung disease and diffuse cutaneous involvement?
questions.concept: Anti-Scl-70 marks diffuse disease with pulmonary fibrosis, anti-centromere marks limited disease with pulmonary arterial hypertension, and anti-RNA polymerase III marks a high risk of renal crisis and occult malignancy.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Rheumatoid arthritis, SLE & connective tissue disease
questions.stem: Mixed connective tissue disease is characterised by which antibody together with overlapping features of lupus, myositis and scleroderma?
questions.concept: High-titre anti-U1 RNP with Raynaud phenomenon, puffy hands, arthritis, myositis and oesophageal dysmotility defines the syndrome, whose principal cause of death is pulmonary arterial hypertension.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Sepsis, fever of unknown origin & antimicrobial stewardship
questions.stem: In the initial resuscitation of septic shock, the recommended crystalloid volume within the first three hours is at least:
questions.concept: The Surviving Sepsis guidance recommends 30 mL/kg of balanced crystalloid for sepsis-induced hypoperfusion, with further fluid guided by dynamic measures of responsiveness rather than fixed targets.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Sepsis, fever of unknown origin & antimicrobial stewardship
questions.stem: Which biomarker trend is most useful for guiding safe de-escalation of antibiotics in sepsis?
questions.concept: Procalcitonin falls quickly when bacterial infection resolves and trials show that procalcitonin-guided stopping shortens antibiotic courses without increasing mortality, whereas C-reactive protein is slower and less specific.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Sepsis, fever of unknown origin & antimicrobial stewardship
questions.stem: Which is the most appropriate approach when blood cultures identify a single organism sensitive to a narrow-spectrum agent?
options: Continue the broad empirical combination to be safe
De-escalate to the narrowest effective agent for the shortest effective duration
Add a second agent for synergy in all cases
Switch to a newer broad-spectrum agent
questions.concept: De-escalation is the core of stewardship, reducing resistance, cost, Clostridioides difficile infection and drug toxicity without compromising outcome once the organism and its sensitivities are known.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Sepsis, fever of unknown origin & antimicrobial stewardship
questions.stem: A patient meets criteria for sepsis but the lactate is normal and blood pressure is maintained. The most important immediate action is:
options: Obtain cultures and give appropriate antibiotics within one hour while seeking source control
questions.concept: Every hour of delay in effective antibiotics increases mortality, and identifying and draining or removing the source is at least as important as the drug choice.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Sepsis, fever of unknown origin & antimicrobial stewardship
questions.stem: Which vasopressor is added when noradrenaline alone fails to reach the mean arterial pressure target in septic shock?
questions.concept: Vasopressin acts on V1 receptors independently of adrenergic pathways, so it is noradrenaline-sparing; dopamine causes more tachyarrhythmia and dobutamine is an inotrope for persistent hypoperfusion despite adequate pressure.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Sepsis, fever of unknown origin & antimicrobial stewardship
questions.stem: Which category of fever of unknown origin should prompt evaluation for drug-induced fever?
options: Fever with a new rash and eosinophilia in a patient on multiple recently started drugs
Fever with weight loss over months
questions.concept: Drug fever often appears one to three weeks after starting the agent, may be accompanied by rash and eosinophilia, and characteristically settles within 72 hours of stopping the culprit, so a careful drug chart review is mandatory.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Sepsis, fever of unknown origin & antimicrobial stewardship
questions.stem: Which imaging modality has the highest yield in classical fever of unknown origin after initial tests are unrevealing?
options: FDG positron emission tomography with CT
questions.concept: Fluorodeoxyglucose uptake highlights occult infection, large-vessel vasculitis and malignancy in a single whole-body study and directs biopsy, giving a diagnostic contribution in roughly half of unexplained cases.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Sepsis, fever of unknown origin & antimicrobial stewardship
questions.stem: Which finding most strongly suggests adult-onset Still disease as a cause of fever of unknown origin?
options: Quotidian fever with an evanescent salmon-pink rash, arthritis and a very high serum ferritin
Fever with a low erythrocyte sedimentation rate
questions.concept: A ferritin many times normal with a low glycosylated fraction, neutrophilic leucocytosis and the transient rash appearing with fever spikes is characteristic, and it is a diagnosis of exclusion requiring infection and malignancy to be ruled out.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Sepsis, fever of unknown origin & antimicrobial stewardship
questions.stem: In sepsis, why is a balanced crystalloid generally preferred to 0.9 percent saline for large-volume resuscitation?
options: It causes less hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis and possibly less renal injury
It expands plasma volume more than saline
questions.concept: The high chloride load of normal saline reduces renal blood flow and causes a hyperchloraemic acidosis, and trials such as SMART showed fewer major adverse kidney events with balanced solutions.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Spondyloarthritis, gout & the vasculitides
questions.stem: Which feature best distinguishes inflammatory from mechanical back pain?
options: Pain worse on exertion and relieved by rest
Morning stiffness over 30 minutes with improvement on exercise and night pain in the second half of the night
questions.concept: Inflammatory back pain begins before 45, improves with movement and worsens with rest, and this pattern with sacroiliitis on imaging or HLA-B27 supports axial spondyloarthritis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Spondyloarthritis, gout & the vasculitides
questions.stem: The first-line pharmacological treatment for axial spondyloarthritis is:
options: Regular NSAIDs with a structured exercise programme
questions.concept: Unlike peripheral arthritis, axial disease does not respond to conventional disease-modifying drugs; NSAIDs plus physiotherapy come first, and biologics targeting tumour necrosis factor or interleukin-17 follow if response is inadequate.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Spondyloarthritis, gout & the vasculitides
questions.stem: Which radiographic change is characteristic of established ankylosing spondylitis of the spine?
options: Symmetrical syndesmophytes producing a bamboo spine with squaring of vertebral bodies
questions.concept: Vertically oriented syndesmophytes arise from ossification of the annulus fibrosus, which is different from the horizontal, bulky osteophytes of spondylosis and from the chunky asymmetrical syndesmophytes of psoriatic disease.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Spondyloarthritis, gout & the vasculitides
questions.stem: Which drug lowers urate by inhibiting the URAT1 transporter and is contraindicated in urolithiasis?
questions.concept: Uricosuric agents block tubular reabsorption so urinary urate rises, which risks stone formation; they also require adequate renal function and high fluid intake to be effective and safe.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Spondyloarthritis, gout & the vasculitides
questions.stem: Urate-lowering therapy started during an acute attack of gout should be accompanied by:
options: Anti-inflammatory prophylaxis with colchicine or an NSAID for several months
Immediate cessation at the first flare
questions.concept: Mobilising crystals from deposits provokes flares in the first months, so prophylaxis improves adherence; treat-to-target dosing to a urate below 6 mg/dL is what actually dissolves tophi.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Spondyloarthritis, gout & the vasculitides
questions.stem: Which crystal is identified in pseudogout, and how does it appear under polarised light?
options: Rhomboid, weakly positively birefringent calcium pyrophosphate
questions.concept: Calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate deposition produces chondrocalcinosis of menisci and the triangular fibrocartilage of the wrist, and attacks favour large joints in the elderly.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Spondyloarthritis, gout & the vasculitides
questions.stem: Asthma, eosinophilia above 10 percent and a necrotising vasculitis with p-ANCA suggest:
questions.concept: The three phases of allergic rhinitis and asthma, then eosinophilic tissue infiltration, then vasculitis with mononeuritis multiplex and cardiac involvement characterise this ANCA-associated disease; cardiac disease drives mortality.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Spondyloarthritis, gout & the vasculitides
questions.stem: Which vasculitis characteristically causes recurrent oral and genital ulceration with uveitis and a positive pathergy test?
questions.concept: Behcet disease is a variable-vessel vasculitis associated with HLA-B51 that uniquely affects both arteries and veins, causing venous thrombosis and pulmonary artery aneurysms alongside the mucocutaneous and ocular features.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Spondyloarthritis, gout & the vasculitides
questions.stem: In giant cell arteritis, which treatment is added to corticosteroids to reduce cumulative steroid exposure and relapse?
questions.concept: The GiACTA trial showed higher sustained remission and lower cumulative steroid dose with tocilizumab; note that it suppresses the erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein, so these can no longer be used to monitor disease activity.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Thyroid disorders
questions.stem: Which pattern of thyroid function tests indicates subclinical hypothyroidism?
options: Raised TSH with a normal free thyroxine
Raised TSH with a low free thyroxine
Low TSH with a raised free thyroxine
Low TSH with a low free thyroxine
questions.concept: The pituitary is the most sensitive detector of thyroid hormone deficiency, so TSH rises before thyroxine falls below the reference range; treatment is considered when TSH exceeds 10 or when antibodies, symptoms or pregnancy are present.
questions.reference: Harrison 21e, Ch. 375 (Disorders of the Thyroid Gland)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Thyroid disorders
questions.stem: In a patient with suspected central hypothyroidism, which test result would be expected?
options: Low free thyroxine with a low or inappropriately normal TSH
Low free thyroxine with a high TSH
High free thyroxine with a low TSH
Normal free thyroxine with a high TSH
questions.concept: Pituitary or hypothalamic failure removes the drive to the thyroid, so TSH cannot rise appropriately; thyroxine must never be started before glucocorticoid replacement because it can precipitate adrenal crisis.
questions.reference: Harrison 21e, Ch. 375 (Disorders of the Thyroid Gland)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Thyroid disorders
questions.stem: Which single test best distinguishes Graves disease from a toxic nodule when the clinical picture is unclear?
options: Radioiodine uptake scan showing diffuse versus focal uptake, or TSH receptor antibody
questions.concept: Diffuse homogeneous uptake with a positive TSH receptor antibody confirms Graves disease, whereas a solitary hot nodule suppressing the rest of the gland indicates a toxic adenoma, and the distinction changes definitive treatment.
questions.reference: Harrison 21e, Ch. 375 (Disorders of the Thyroid Gland)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Thyroid disorders
questions.stem: A pregnant woman in the first trimester is found to have suppressed TSH with a mildly raised free thyroxine and no goitre or eye signs. The most likely explanation is:
options: Gestational transient thyrotoxicosis from human chorionic gonadotropin cross-stimulation
questions.concept: Human chorionic gonadotropin shares an alpha subunit with TSH and weakly stimulates its receptor, peaking at 10 to 12 weeks; the picture resolves spontaneously and needs no antithyroid drug.
questions.reference: Harrison 21e, Ch. 375 (Disorders of the Thyroid Gland)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Thyroid disorders
questions.stem: Which feature of Graves ophthalmopathy is an indication for urgent high-dose corticosteroids and possible orbital decompression?
options: Optic neuropathy with reduced colour vision
questions.concept: Compressive optic neuropathy at the orbital apex threatens permanent visual loss, so it is treated urgently; smoking cessation and selenium have roles in milder disease and radioiodine can worsen active eye disease.
questions.reference: Harrison 21e, Ch. 375 (Disorders of the Thyroid Gland)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Thyroid disorders
questions.stem: Amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis type 2 differs from type 1 in that it:
options: Results from iodine-induced excess synthesis in a nodular gland
Is a destructive thyroiditis with a low vascularity on Doppler, responding to corticosteroids
questions.concept: Type 1 is iodine-driven hyperfunction treated with thionamides, whereas type 2 is drug-induced destruction releasing preformed hormone and responds to steroids; distinguishing them changes management entirely.
questions.reference: Harrison 21e, Ch. 375 (Disorders of the Thyroid Gland)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Thyroid disorders
questions.stem: A solitary thyroid nodule with fine needle aspiration reported as Bethesda category IV, a follicular neoplasm, should be managed by:
questions.concept: Cytology cannot distinguish follicular adenoma from carcinoma because that rests on capsular invasion, so lobectomy provides the histology; molecular marker panels can reduce unnecessary surgery.
questions.reference: Harrison 21e, Ch. 375 (Disorders of the Thyroid Gland)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Thyroid disorders
questions.stem: Which finding on a thyroid nodule biopsy would indicate medullary carcinoma and prompt screening for phaeochromocytoma?
options: Sheets of cells with amyloid stroma and positive calcitonin staining
questions.concept: Medullary carcinoma arises from parafollicular C cells and may be part of MEN 2, so RET testing and exclusion of phaeochromocytoma are mandatory before any neck surgery to avoid an intraoperative hypertensive crisis.
questions.reference: Harrison 21e, Ch. 375 (Disorders of the Thyroid Gland)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Thyroid disorders
questions.stem: In a critically ill patient, a low free triiodothyronine with a normal or low TSH and a raised reverse triiodothyronine indicates:
questions.concept: Illness shifts deiodination from the active to the inactive pathway; treating with thyroxine has not improved outcomes, so thyroid function is best rechecked after recovery rather than acted on during the acute illness.
questions.reference: Harrison 21e, Ch. 375 (Disorders of the Thyroid Gland)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Tubulointerstitial disease, RTA & renal replacement therapy
questions.stem: Which acid-base and potassium pattern characterises type 2 (proximal) renal tubular acidosis?
options: Hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis with hypokalaemia and a bicarbonate threshold that is reset lower
High anion gap acidosis with hyperkalaemia
questions.concept: Failure of proximal bicarbonate reclamation causes bicarbonate wasting until plasma bicarbonate falls to the new lower threshold, after which the urine can be acidified, unlike distal disease where it cannot.
questions.reference: Harrison 21e, Ch. 315 (Tubulointerstitial Diseases of the Kidney)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Tubulointerstitial disease, RTA & renal replacement therapy
questions.stem: Which drug most characteristically causes chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis with a bland urinary sediment and slowly rising creatinine?
questions.concept: Lithium enters principal cells through the epithelial sodium channel and causes nephrogenic diabetes insipidus with chronic interstitial fibrosis and microcysts, so renal function and concentrating ability need long-term monitoring.
questions.reference: Harrison 21e, Ch. 315 (Tubulointerstitial Diseases of the Kidney)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Tubulointerstitial disease, RTA & renal replacement therapy
questions.stem: Which vascular access provides the best long-term survival for maintenance haemodialysis?
questions.concept: A native fistula has the lowest rates of infection and thrombosis and the best patency, which is why forearm veins are preserved from venepuncture in patients approaching end-stage renal disease.
questions.reference: Harrison 21e, Ch. 315 (Tubulointerstitial Diseases of the Kidney)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Tubulointerstitial disease, RTA & renal replacement therapy
questions.stem: A patient develops acute kidney injury with sterile pyuria, eosinophiluria and a rash a week after starting a proton pump inhibitor. The management is:
options: Withdraw the offending drug, with corticosteroids if renal function does not recover
questions.concept: Acute interstitial nephritis is a hypersensitivity reaction, so removing the trigger is essential; steroids are used when function fails to improve, and delayed diagnosis leads to interstitial fibrosis.
questions.reference: Harrison 21e, Ch. 315 (Tubulointerstitial Diseases of the Kidney)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Tubulointerstitial disease, RTA & renal replacement therapy
questions.stem: Which feature suggests that hyperkalaemia is due to type 4 rather than type 1 renal tubular acidosis?
options: Hyperkalaemia with a mild acidosis in a diabetic with hyporeninaemic hypoaldosteronism
questions.concept: Type 4 reflects aldosterone deficiency or resistance, so potassium is high and the acidosis mild; type 1 causes hypokalaemia with an inappropriately alkaline urine, nephrocalcinosis and stones.
questions.reference: Harrison 21e, Ch. 315 (Tubulointerstitial Diseases of the Kidney)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Tubulointerstitial disease, RTA & renal replacement therapy
questions.stem: Which complication of long-term haemodialysis is caused by beta-2 microglobulin deposition?
options: Dialysis-related amyloidosis with carpal tunnel syndrome and destructive arthropathy
questions.concept: Beta-2 microglobulin is poorly cleared by conventional low-flux membranes, and its amyloid deposits in synovium, bone cysts and the carpal tunnel; high-flux membranes and transplantation reduce the risk.
questions.reference: Harrison 21e, Ch. 315 (Tubulointerstitial Diseases of the Kidney)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Tubulointerstitial disease, RTA & renal replacement therapy
questions.stem: Which finding indicates that chronic kidney disease has caused secondary hyperparathyroidism with high-turnover bone disease?
options: Low phosphate with low parathyroid hormone
High phosphate, low calcitriol and a markedly raised parathyroid hormone
High calcium with low parathyroid hormone
questions.concept: Reduced renal 1-alpha-hydroxylation lowers calcitriol while phosphate retention and FGF23 rise, together driving parathyroid hyperplasia; management is phosphate binders, active vitamin D analogues and calcimimetics.
questions.reference: Harrison 21e, Ch. 315 (Tubulointerstitial Diseases of the Kidney)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Tubulointerstitial disease, RTA & renal replacement therapy
questions.stem: Which condition causes a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis with a positive urinary anion gap and a urine pH above 5.5 despite systemic acidaemia?
options: Proximal (type 2) renal tubular acidosis after bicarbonate depletion
questions.concept: The failure of the alpha-intercalated cell hydrogen ATPase means ammonium excretion is impaired, so the urinary anion gap is positive and the urine cannot be acidified, in contrast to diarrhoea where ammonium excretion rises and the gap is negative.
questions.reference: Harrison 21e, Ch. 315 (Tubulointerstitial Diseases of the Kidney)
